items.title: Caveman Make Loop: Model Harness Different
items.content:
TL;DR : Running Recursive's new Flint model in Oh My Pi (OMP) was a looping disaster of telegraphic "caveman speak." But running the exact same user prompt in OpenCode was night-and-day articulate and competent. The contrast sent me digging through session traces and harness prompts—and reconsidering how quickly I'd judged the model.

At work, I just got a new MacBook Pro with 64GB RAM and an M5 Max CPU. Just in time for news about M6 CPUs , but oh well. Still, I'm told this should be pretty capable at running local AI models.

So, lately, I’ve been jumping between two harnesses: OpenCode and Oh My Pi (OMP) . Both seem capable, but have different designs and flavors. OpenCode feels like a structured, modular developer workbench. OMP aims at raw terminal speed, token frugality, and minimal ceremony. I haven't done an exhaustive code comparison, so these are just vibey impressions.

At the same time, I’ve been running Flint , an open-weight model released by Recursive Superintelligence . To serve the model locally, I've been using rec , Recursive's own inference engine, which exposes local OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints.

The label on the tin says Flint is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 40 billion total parameters, but only ~2.5 billion active parameters per token. It uses 4-bit NVFP4 output layer quantization, allowing the full model to fit and execute in unified memory on Apple Silicon via Metal kernels.

In my own runs, actual decode throughput (pure generation speed, excluding prompt prefill and tool execution waits) clocked in around 60–80 tokens per second across sustained agent turns. I'm still wrapping my head around expected performance for local models on this machine, but this seems really good.

Of course, speed doesn't mean anything if the model is busy spewing garbage the whole time. So, I decided to put Flint through its paces on a real-world task: running an issue triage pass on the DecafClaw backlog using ghflow .

A quick word on ghflow : it's an agent skill I've been building to automate project workflows on GitHub. Instead of me manually clicking through project boards, labeling issues, branching worktrees, and writing pull request summaries, ghflow gives an agent a structured set of reference procedures to triage, scope, and deliver issues.

In a full-scale unattended burndown using a cloud model, ghflow often relies on subagents to parallelize work. But with this local model setup, driving concurrent subagents led to endless KV-Cache thrashing—chewing up GPU time recalculating prompt prefills much like frequent multi-material filament changes on my 3D printer with the MMU3 .

So to lean into consistent caching, I explicitly instructed the agent to triage serially in a single session:

@ghflow Let's triage issues not yet triaged, those without triage:* labels. Do so without using subagents, because we're only running one local model and cannot handle parallel requests

Attempt one: The caveman doom loop in OMP

My first run with Flint in OMP was a disaster—here's how it started "thinking":

We need respond/action. User invoked ghflow, asks triage untriaged issues.

Need follow skill. We need inspect. We have no actual tools listed beyond current,

but likely can use. Need likely task triage-issues. Must load task reference and

shared context perhaps. Need not ask. Need gather state. Since they mention

long list untriaged. Need run ghflow facts perhaps. First must read selected task

Most auxiliary verbs, articles, and copulas have been dropped, leaving a staccato stream of verbs and nouns. I've heard of this caveman thing as an attempt to conserve tokens—i.e. " why use many token when few token do trick ". But, I don't think this was intentionally that. And even if it was, it didn't work.

I let it keep going, if only to see what it would do. After 100 turns, I think the agent had entered what looked like an attractor basin :

Turn 101: think: ["We need continue. Need understand todo…

items.title: Software Line Specialist
items.summary: satire
items.content:
This is a code-only role; for AI-native jobs, please look at our other listings

We’re looking for a senior software line specialist, in TypeScript !

ACME Inc. is a fast-growing startup helping small businesses monitor their financials. We work with business owners across the globe, turning their feedback into actionable insights. Backed by Maltese Falcon Capital, we recently raised a $15M Series A to bring effortless monitoring to every brick-and-mortar store.

You’ll be joining a high-performance, close-knit team of AI natives! We’ve been AI-first for the past 2 years, with every part of the product agent-friendly and interconnected: design, development, QA, CI/CD, infra, data analysis. We like to say that our stack is English!

While English has gotten us 99.5% of the way there, we’re in need of a hands-on engineer ready to close the final 0.5%. Over time, we’ve noticed some issues that are immune to prompts and catch agents in loops. Sometimes, the issue at hand gets fixed, but it results in another issue. This is where you step in. As a line specialist, your job will be to investigate and fix complex issues, primarily by reading the underlying code.

We’re looking for someone ready to open an IDE and dive deep into an unknown codebase — a fearless detective who is comfortable inspecting logs and database rows, and has the know-how to piece all the information together. The perfect candidate should be willing to work on a problem for hours, sometimes even days.

This is a new position for us. We expect someone who works autonomously, makes sound decisions independently and takes full ownership of their work. We are happy to help in any way we can (you’ll have access to agents’ reasoning traces), but ultimately we depend on your confidence in understanding the problem and shipping a solution.

read the codebase, go over application logs, query the database

prepare, test, review and ship fixes by yourself

occasionally consult on unreleased features

onboard and mentor a future junior line specialist

have at least 5 years of pre-2022 TypeScript experience

are comfortable running tests manually and using a “debugger”

can work on a problem with sustained attention for hours

are autonomous and an independent thinker

previous experience as a line specialist

DB administration experience (our agents say it’s Postgres)

multiple-choice questions (e.g. you’re given a TypeScript expression, choose the correct result)

explain concepts in your own words (for example, ACID)

application with an intentional defect; candidates are required to find and fix the issue without the use of AI

We feel it prudent to point out that you will be allowed to work on one thing at a time in this role. While parallel development is the default, we understand line specialists prefer to tackle problems in a single-threaded manner, so we will do our best to provide a distraction-free environment for your best work.

To be clear, this role does not include feature development. You’re welcome to look at our AI-native listings if you have more interest in such work!

items.title: The Cybertruck is dead, makes way for Cybercab says Elon Musk
items.content:
Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs , most likely.

Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019 , back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup’s unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.

The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

But development of the Cybertruck was more troubled than usual for Tesla, which struggled heavily to bring both the Model 3 and Y into mass production. Musk demanded “ Lego-like precision ” from the workers assembling the trucks, but achieving the 10-micron tolerances required by the Danish toy company was not evidently successful, based on what we saw when we experienced our first Cybertruck in reality .

That was in 2023, when Cybertruck headlines were mostly about recalls and stop sales. By then, the truck used a conventional unibody chassis—conventional for Tesla, not for full-size pickup trucks. Toward the end of that year, Musk told his audience that “ we dug our grave ” with the truck, perhaps the first public acknowledgment that annual sales of a quarter of a million Cybertrucks probably wasn’t going to happen after all.

Sales never took off , and the Cybertruck’s divisive shape became an all-too-visible reminder of the CEO’s role in reshaping the federal government to his liking . Even selling thousands of Cybertrucks to SpaceX couldn’t save the pickup. Now, with America having vociferously rejected Musk’s vision of governance, those wishing to drive something that reminds everyone around them of that vision will only have a few months more to purchase one.

Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

items.summary: apl, plt
items.content:
Last week I attended IFL2026 , which was

probably one of the best conference experiences I have ever had. One of the many

good presentations was by Michael Haddon , who

demonstration language called Lane, but it inspired me to think more carefully

about nondeterminism in Futhark (there is some), and what it might cost to get

I often use the terms “determinism” or “deterministic” when explaining why I

think data parallel programming is such a good paradigm, so perhaps it is

surprising to see me write a blog post about nondeterminism in Futhark. But as

is so often the case with such bold promises, they often tend to get a little

weaker once you look closely enough. Michael Haddon’s work defines some

nomenclature that is helpful for this discussion:

Exact means that the computation produces the same result every time,

guaranteed. (Michael describes this as matching the “serial reference”, which

I think is not the best way of looking at it, but that’s a question of

Replay means that if you rerun the computation with the same “schedule”

(in some sense “machine”), you will get the same result, but other machines

Approx means potentially nondeterministic results.

The kind of nondeterminism we are talking about here is not the kind of

free-form nondeterminism that arises from classic shared-state concurrent

programming. Indeed, both Lane and Futhark are pretty much exclusively concerned

with the kind of nondeterminism that arises from floating-point rounding errors.

The simplest example is the non-associativity of addition:

If we have an array of numbers we need to sum, then the result depends on the

order in which you sum them. When parallelising a summation, you often do things

like split the numbers into blocks, sum each block on a separate processor, then

combine the partial results. This changes the order of addition, and hence the

result. Now, an important point is that there is no reason to think that the

parallelised result is numerically worse than a serial left-to-right

summation, but it will be different. Further, an efficient implementation will

likely choose a number of chunks somewhat proportional to the number of

processors on the machine, which means the result may also be different on other

machines (but again, not necessarily worse ). This corresponds to the “Replay”

class of nondeterminism. Finally, the partial results may be combined using

resolved in a different order when the program is rerun on the same machine.

Even in this simple example of summing a bunch of numbers, we encounter both

classes of nondeterminism. Note that none of them are “race conditions” in the

usual sense of the program sometimes just malfunctioning : the point is that

the result changes, but given that the result is in some sense already “wrong”

(due to roundoff error), the main issue is that there are cases where we care

about getting the same “wrong” result every time.

So in Futhark, ostensibly a deterministic language, where does the

nondeterminism come from? There are a few sources. Some of them come when

programmers violate mandated constraints (but which are unchecked for various

reasons), and others are basically down to floating-point roundoff error.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Global stocks tumble as AI panic grips markets; US adds 165,000 new jobs in October
items.content:
With European stock markets closed after a nervy day, and Wall Street calmer than yesterday, it’s time to wrap up…

European stock markets fell sharply today as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets overnight. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.

US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had recovered to a 1% fall, helped by a bounce in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.

Across Europe, there were similar losses: Germany’s Dax index has fallen by 2%, France’s Cac 40 has lost 0.8%, and Spain’s Ibex ended the day down 0.6%. Italy’s FTSE Mib fell 0.9%.

In Asia-Pacific markets, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sunk 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 6.5%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Over in New York right now, the Nasdaq is up 1.5% (having fallen by 5.5% yesterday), and the S&P 500 is up 0.7%.

items.summary: lisp
items.content:
The difficulty in learning Clojure does not stem from its syntax, which happens to be extremely simple, but from having to learn new methods for solving problems. As such, we'll focus on understanding the core concepts and how they can be combined to solve problems the functional way.

All the mainstream languages belong to the same family. Once you learn one of these languages there is very little effort involved in learning another. Generally, all you have to do is learn some syntax sugar and the useful functions in the standard library to become productive. There might be a new concept here and there, but most of your existing skills are easily transferable.

This is not the case with Clojure. Being a Lisp dialect, it comes from a different family of languages and requires learning new concepts in order to use effectively. There is no reason to be discouraged if the code appears hard to read at first. I assure you that the syntax is not inherently difficult to understand, and that with a bit of practice you might find it to be quite the opposite.

The goal of this guide is to provide an overview of the core concepts necessary to become productive with Clojure. Let's start by examining some of the key advantages of the functional style and why you would want to learn a functional language in the first place.

Clojure is a functional language. This makes it extremely well positioned for writing large applications. As the application grows it's imperative to be able to reason about its constituent parts in isolation. Conversely, there is a lot of value in building code out of components that are testable and reusable by nature. Let's take a look at why the functional approach is such a good fit here.

Functional languages are ideal for writing large applications because they eschew global state and favor immutability as the default. Having immutable shared state allows us to safely reason about parts of the application in isolation. At first glance, the idea of using immutable data structures sounds unnecessarily restrictive. However, as we'll soon see, many of the benefits associated with the functional style stem directly from it.

Mutable data can either be passed around by value or by reference. The safe approach would be to pass the data by value as it guarantees that any changes to the data will remain in the local scope. Unfortunately, this approach is extremely inefficient, so most languages pass data by reference instead.

Passing data by reference is fast, but it makes the code difficult to reason about. In order to safely work with the data you have to know all the places where it might be referenced. The complexity grows with the size of the application. The more code has access to a piece of data the more proverbial balls you end up having to juggle in your head.

Immutable data structures provide us with an ingenious alternative to the above dilemma. Every time a change is made to the data structure a revision is created. We now have the same guarantees offered by naive copying of the data, but we only pay the price proportional to the size of the change.

Just like garbage collection frees us from having to manually track data allocation and deallocation, immutable data structures free us from having to manage data references by hand. From the user perspective we simply "copy" the data any time we make a change. The language will take care of figuring out what parts of it can be cleaned up when they're no longer used.

Having such data structures facilitates writing pure functions. A pure function is simply a function without side effects. These functions do not rely on any state outside their inputs and they do not modify any external state when they run. Given the same parameters, the function will always produce the same result, regardless of the global state of the application.

items.title: Revisiting Buttons and Cursors
items.content:
The CSS Working Group resolved to use cursor: pointer for buttons and other clickable form controls in the new appearance: base styles. That happened on October 21, but I posted about it yesterday and, uh, people have feelings about cursors.

I wrote about buttons and cursors back in 2022, when a post titled "Buttons shouldn't have a hand cursor" was making the rounds. I admitted I didn't have a strong opinion either way, then argued that not using the hand cursor had become the new anti-pattern anyway. The web isn't an operating system, and people expect clickable things to show a hand.

The issue is Cursors For Base Appearance in CSS Forms Level 1. The group adopted the rules from this comment , and the part that's triggering half the Web is:

select, option, input[type=checkbox], input[type=radio],

button, input[type=button], input[type=submit], input[type=reset],

input[type=color], input[type=image], ::file-selector-button {

It seems like we have a tabs vs. spaces sort of debate. Again.

Nicole Sullivan pulled cursor data from a bunch of design systems and, in September, 27 of the 33 systems that set a cursor used pointer . After she added more systems, it was closer to a 50/50 split. Elika Etemad made the usability case in the meeting. Per the minutes, she said the hand "makes it clear, as soon as you're hovering an interactive control, you're supposed to click on it," and called it a "usability benefit even if not historically done on some platforms."

His point is that he can't tell whether ⌘-clicking something will open it in a new window anymore. He feels more confident clicking a button when he knows it won't change the URL, like when it just opens a popover or a panel. He's not wrong about that.*

I replied that I've been on team evil since 2022 (albeit without a strong opinion, just following what users seem to expect). Touch screens don't have a cursor at all, and on desktop, browsers show a link's URL in the corner when you hover it. That's some type of hint, at least.

Haz pushed back that he'd have to watch the bottom-left corner with his peripheral vision, which is fair. He also said he never cared which cursor buttons got, he just wanted links to have their own. I can appreciate that.

Jacob Paris liked the standard cursor on buttons because it makes web apps feel more like desktop apps than websites. My opinion hasn't changed, though. People have already learned that a hand cursor means clickable on the Web. It's by no means mandatory, but it's familiar and satisfying, so it stuck.

Either way, nothing changes today. The resolution only covers appearance: base , which browsers haven't shipped yet. Buttons and selects still use appearance: auto , and their cursor is still default . If your CSS reset, design system, or web components already set cursor: pointer on buttons, keep it.

When appearance: base ships, controls that opt in will get the same cursors by default. But remember, these are only defaults! You can still add whatever cursor you want to whatever element you want. Nobody's gonna stop you.**

In 2022 , I said I'd keep changing the cursor on buttons until there's a good reason to stop. In 2026, I still haven't found one…and neither has the CSS Working Group.

items.content:
An IPv4 address is just a 32-bit number, and glibc will accept it in forms you would never recognize. ⁰𝑋⁴5．🯰３₆。⁵₂₈𝟲🯶 is one of them. Anything that judges an address by how it looks can be walked around.

That is a real ping, to a real box, and it got a real reply. The thing after ping -c1 is a mix of LCD segmented digits, superscripts, subscripts, circled digits, a double-struck X and math-alphabet digits, with nine invisible characters that my terminal drew as white boxes because it had no idea what else to do with them. Paste it into a terminal and it looks like line noise. Hand it to getaddrinfo() and it is 69.30.206.130 .

Every example in this post points at the same server, 69.30.206.130 . It answers ping, and it serves exactly one page, /poc.html , on its bare IP so you can prove the HTTP side works too. Every screenshot is real output, captured on Ubuntu 24.04 with glibc 2.39, iputils 20240117 and curl 8.5.0.

Start with the boring part, which is already weirder than most people expect. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit unsigned integer. The dotted quad is just how we have agreed to write it down. The parser that turns text into that integer is inet_aton() , and its rules date back to 4.2BSD. In glibc it lives in resolv/inet_addr.c , and each part is read like this:

Base 0 means strtoul() picks the base from the prefix: 0x is hex, a leading 0 is octal, anything else is decimal. Each dotted part gets its own prefix, so you can mix bases inside one address. Then there is the part count:

One part is the whole 32-bit number. Two parts are an 8-bit network and a 24-bit host. Three parts are 8, 8 and 16 bits. These were meant for the old class A/B/C networks, and nobody ever took them out. Leading zeros are unlimited too, as long as the value still fits.

Everything above is well known. It is the reason SSRF filters are supposed to parse addresses instead of regexing them. The fun starts with a flag most people never look at: AI_IDN .

AI_IDN is a glibc extension that tells getaddrinfo() the name might be an internationalized domain name, so it should be converted to ASCII before lookup. ping sets it, because iputils is built with IDN support. Here is what glibc does with it, in sysdeps/posix/getaddrinfo.c :

Look at the order. The IDNA conversion runs first , and the numeric address parser only sees the output. __idna_to_dns_encoding() hands the string to libidn2, which applies UTS #46 mapping. UTS #46 exists so that a user typing a domain in a different width or style still lands on the same name. To do that it folds a huge range of compatibility characters down to plain ASCII. That table does not care that the result is going to be read as a number.

Digits are covered, and so are the dots. The x in a hex prefix and the a – f hex letters are covered too, which means every one of the classic forms above can be rebuilt out of Unicode lookalikes:

Circled two-digit numbers are a nice touch: ⑥⑨.㉚.⑳⑥.⑬⓪ is four characters shorter than the plain address it decodes to. Hex works the same way, with a bold script x for the prefix, a Roman numeral one hundred standing in for c , and modifier letters for e :

Notice that ping echoes back 0x451ece82 in its PING line. ping also asks for AI_CANONIDN , so what it prints is the name after IDNA mapping. That is the clearest view you will get of what the resolver actually parsed.

Nothing says a single address has to stick to one style. The mapping is done one character at a time, so every digit, dot and hex letter can come from a different block. items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: HackerTube – a clean way to browse videos recommended on Hacker News
items.content:
A HackerTube directory for the curious. Talks, rabbit holes, and ideas worth your time — recommended by the people of Hacker News.

Remember when finding something on the web felt like a recommendation from a friend? HackerTube brings a little of that feeling back. This HackerTube browser starts with conversations: someone has a question, someone else remembers a talk, and a useful video gets passed along. Across years of discussions, those small recommendations become a remarkably interesting library.

Hacker Tubes lets you explore that open collection without an account. Begin with the HackerTube daily mix , follow your curiosity through a topic, or keep a few discoveries for the weekend. The interface stays simple so the videos can do the talking. There are no paid placements in this directory, and the selection is based on the provided recommendation data.

Start with a fresh page of thumbnails. The HackerTube daily order changes at midnight UTC, balancing variety with the strength of repeated recommendations. Move through pages to discover older lectures alongside newer explainers. The archive is a snapshot, so a fresh mix means a new selection from existing videos, rather than a promise of newly uploaded videos every day.

Search a title, creator, subject, or phrase. HackerTube topics cover programming, mathematics, science, design, history, and much more. Combine search with a topic and, when verified runtimes are available, a length filter. A narrow search is useful when you know what you want; a broad category is better when you want to be surprised.

Open a thumbnail to watch the video and read why HN recommended it. Add it to watch later or explicitly mark it watched. HackerTube keeps that library in this browser, and you can undo either choice. A click on a thumbnail alone does not count as finishing a video. Hide watched items when you want a page of unfamiliar ideas.

A large view count does not explain why a talk matters. HackerTube cards include a summary, recommendation counts, and the reason a community member might point you toward it. Where a source quote exists, the player links directly to the original HN comment. Read that context before committing an hour, and judge the recommendation for yourself.

The video grid comes first. Hover over a thumbnail, focus it with the keyboard, or tap it on a touch screen to reveal the title and creator. HackerTube uses plain controls, readable type, and straightforward pagination. You can browse at your own pace without an endless feed. On small screens the directory adapts while keeping useful controls within reach.

Save something interesting without interrupting the video you are already watching. HackerTube watch later and watched collections are separate, and the hide-watched switch helps avoid repeat discoveries. Local storage keeps these choices on this device. Clearing browser data removes them, and private browsing may discard them when its session ends. The collection does not require an email address.

Explore programming talks, systems explanations, language design, and practical demonstrations. A HackerTube recommendation can offer a second explanation of a familiar idea or an introduction to something entirely new. Use HN favorites when you want talks that have come up repeatedly across the archive, then switch back to daily discovery when you want a wider range.

Save a few promising videos, compare their summaries, and return after watching to mark your progress. Recommendations are a starting point for study, not a curriculum or a guarantee of accuracy.

items.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
items.content:
On February 10th, 1996, a computer program (IBM's Deep Blue)

defeated the reigning chess champion (Garry Kasparov) in a game of chess for the first time.

Deep Blue would go on to lose the match,

but a year later, would get its revenge in a 3.5-2.5 rematch.

In order to achieve this feat, IBM spent several million dollars on research and

development building a special-purpose computer specifically for this purpose.

Deep Blue itself (the victorious, upgraded version)

was powered by 30 P2SC processors each running at roughly 120 MHz,

and (most importantly) 480 custom VLSI chess co-processors used to perform chess-specific

operations like move generation and position evaluation.

When it was built, Deep Blue was the 259th most powerful supercomputer in the world,

and could analyze over 200 million chess positions per second.

But was Deep Blue necessary to beat Kasparov?

Or could we have gotten away with an off-the-shelf 1996 desktop

As it turns out, we could easily have beaten Kasparov without building Deep Blue, using only commodity hardware,

and it (almost certainly) wouldn't have even been close.

I know this because, as I write this very sentence, I have sitting next to me a

200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro (released exactly 31 years ago---November 1st, 1995) with 64MB of RAM

running a custom port of Stockfish that plays at an estimated Elo of

3300 ± 87 at classical time controls---far beyond the strength of any human, or indeed Kasparov's Elo of just under 2800.

But wait, there's more! I've hooked this machine up to the internet with a Realtek RTL8139C Ethernet card,

There are three ways to get stronger at chess: you can

analyze more moves, analyze better moves, or analyze moves better .

Famously, humans improve by doing the latter two:

the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number

of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and

Chess engines like Stockfish , running on silicon instead of our human brains,

and analyze millions of positions per second.

And because there's not that much room for micro-optimizations on modern engines that will let a given

most progress in chess AI also tends to follow how humans improve and finds better methods

for selecting moves and analyzing boards.

Skill in chess is measured by an Elo score.

A difference of 200 Elo means that you should expect the stronger

player to win three out of every four games, and multiplicatively from there: a 400 Elo gap corresponds

to a 90% expected score and a 1000 Elo gap gives a 99.7% expected score.

The best chess engines that you could run on commodity 1996 hardware were rated roughly 2300 Elo.

In contrast, modern Stockfish is rated closer to 3700.

This raises the question: how much of the advantage of a modern chess engine comes down

to the fact that a modern desktop computer is extremely fast, and how much of the

advantage comes down to the fact that we've just gotten better at programming chess engines?

As it turns out, the majority of the Elo gains (+720 of the +1335 gained) can be attributed to better programming,

The first experiment uses Crafty , a competitive engine from 1996

On my Pentium Pro, the 1996 build of Crafty version 11.13 has an Elo of 1999 ± 90 at 1 second per move, and 2383 ± 77 at 10 seconds per move.

On modern hardware (a Ryzen 7) this engine's Elo jumps massively to 2614 ± 97 at the same 1 second per move.

But if I take this engine and slowly start to add all the knowledge we have about

how to design better chess engines---adding modern search algorithms like fail-soft, LMR, correction history; adding better quiescence methods; and adding neural-net evals (NNUE)---then you can

increase the Elo up to 2718 ± 34 on the Pentium Pro at 1 second per move, and 2974 ± 74 at 10 seconds per move.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-50240 📢 Source: redhat 💣 CVSS Score: 8.8 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True A flaw was found in OpenShift Pipelines-as-Code (PAC). PAC does not verify whether the creator of a Repository custom resource has permission to create PipelineRuns. A namespace user with only Repository and Secret create/delete permissions can cause PAC to execute attacker-controlled PipelineRuns as the auto-provisioned pipeline ServiceAccount, which carries ClusterRole/edit by default. This results in namespace-scoped privilege escalation, enabling Secret read, resource creation/modification/deletion, and potential supply chain injection in CI/CD namespaces. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-06T21:53:53.997Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50240
